name: Neck posture / forward head correction

lead: Forward head posture is when the head sits ahead of the shoulders, so the chin appears to poke forward. People work on correcting it to line the chin and neck up better and show a sharper jawline and profile when upright.

It is common with heavy screen use and is usually measured with the craniovertebral angle. Most research on it concerns neck pain, headache and disability, and a 2019 meta-analysis found a correlation with neck pain in adults but not in adolescents. Forum posters disagree on the look: some say correction improves the profile, others say a chin tuck can make a recessed chin look less prominent. No published study has tested its effect on facial appearance.

paras: Correction usually means postural habits, ergonomic changes (screen height, seating) and neck and upper-back strengthening and stretching exercises. People check progress with side-view photos taken from the same distance.

Posture exercises are generally low risk and are studied mainly in the context of neck pain. Some forum users report that a strong chin tuck makes a recessed chin look less prominent, so results in photos can vary by person.

web.title: Neck posture / forward head correction — Grokipedia

chain: Chin and neck line up better
angle.text: Pulling the head back over the shoulders lines the chin and neck up better, which proponents say sharpens the jawline and profile. Posture correction is well studied for neck pain; its effect on how the chin and jaw look has not been tested. Forum users disagree on whether it helps or hurts a recessed chin.

lead: Forward head posture (FHP), sometimes called 'text neck' or 'nerd neck', is a posture in which the head sits forward of the shoulders, so the ear falls in front of a vertical line through the shoulder and the chin appears to poke forward [1][2]. It is usually assessed clinically with the craniovertebral angle, formed between a horizontal line at the seventh cervical vertebra and a line to the ear [2].

Most published research on forward head posture concerns neck pain, headache and disability rather than appearance [3][4][5]. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis examined the relationship between forward head posture and neck pain [6]. Wikipedia reports that this meta-analysis found a correlation in adults but not in adolescents [1].

In looksmaxxing communities, head posture is discussed as something that changes how the chin, jawline and profile look, and the claims run in both directions: some say correcting posture improves the profile, others say it makes a recessed chin look worse. No published study located for this article has tested whether posture correction changes facial appearance.
infobox: Text neck, nerd neck, tech neck
Craniovertebral angle (smaller angle = more forward head) [2]

paras: Wikipedia describes forward head posture as visible when the head sits ahead of the shoulders with the chin protruding, and links it to a hunched upper back; it attributes the recent rise mainly to prolonged use of laptops, tablets and phones, and notes it is also common in certain occupations [1]. It also lists medical conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis and Parkinson's disease that increase upper-back curvature [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, adds that muscles at the back of the skull and the front of the neck can shorten while deep neck flexors weaken, a pattern called upper crossed syndrome [2].

Cross-sectional studies have examined head posture in people with neck pain. One study of 62 patients with neck pain and 52 controls measured the craniovertebral angle and compared it with pain and disability scores [3]. Studies in headache have compared posture and upper neck muscle performance in people with and without headache [4][5][7][8]. A study of healthy adults aged 20 to 50 examined how common forward head, rounded shoulders and kyphosis were and whether they were associated with pain [9].

Wikipedia also cites reported links to cervicogenic headache and overuse pain, and an estimate that each inch of forward head position adds about 10 pounds of load to the cervical spine [1]. These associations concern pain and function; they are not about facial appearance.

Approaches listed by Wikipedia include physical therapy, strengthening, ergonomic changes, regular breaks, manipulation and massage [1]. One randomized study of 58 people with chronic neck pain compared two neck exercise programs for their effect on sitting posture during a distracting task [10].

No studies found on whether correcting forward head posture changes the appearance of the chin, jawline or facial profile. Related research has examined posture in neck pain, headache and office workers [3][4][10][11], including a field comparison of neck and shoulder postures in office workers with and without symptoms [11]. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the relationship between forward head posture and neck pain [6].

On looksmax.org, one poster asked whether correcting forward head posture is 'cope', noting that many models and actors have it; a reply suggested they adopt it for photographs to improve their profile. Another poster asked whether years of forward head posture while gaming might have affected maxillary growth. A thread presenting forward head posture as a source of problems throughout the body links to an article and asks for experiences after fixing posture. A third thread argues that a recessed chin or jaw can cause forward head posture to keep the airway open, and that doing a chin tuck then makes the chin look absent. These are community claims, and research on posture and facial form has not been summarised in the sources reviewed here.

lore.intro: Head posture is discussed on looksmax.org both as a profile-improving fix and as a factor that interacts with a recessed jaw.
